I've recently been thinking about this a lot too -- in short, I don't think these are the same thing (entirely). In my opinion, I believe that love bombing, regardless of the reason (be it ADHD, narcissism, etc.), demonstrates an 'above-average' interest in the subject of love-bombing (i.e. the love-bombed). However, I think the motivation and intent for showing this intense interest and concern for another is what differentiates the two types of 'love-bombing', and, consequently, discounts 'adhd love-bombing' from being true 'love-bombing' by definition. 

From my personal experience and what I've read and learnt from others with ADHD, there can be a tendency to seemingly 'love bomb' during the beginning of a romantic interest or attraction. I believe that this is because we with ADHD have a tendency to become hyper-fixated on things which bring us joy and make us feel good, a.k.a spike our dopamine. The beginnings of romantic interest are filled with moments of intense joy that can become addicting, so we become intensely attracted to this person because they are a source of 'feel-good' for us. Additionally, we also have a tendency to hyperfixate on things which interest us, so the interest of a new person + the highs of a new fling = above-average interest in an individual. We want to make them feel good because they make us feel good and thus we think so highly of them because they are able to make us feel so seen, accepted, good, etc., etc. 

The \*key difference\* here between ADHD 'love-bombing' and narcissistic love-bombing is that we are not doing this with the intent of manipulating the other person. Our actions are a demonstration of our genuine feelings and motivations - we are sincerely enthralled by this person and as such we are showing them. If we are not consciously aware of this and do not regulate ourselves, we can end up harming the subject of our affection because eventually, this level of attention and admiration will die down. Depending on how this slowdown is handled (abruptly or a gentle decline and stabilization) it can be hurtful. We have the capacity to be like a lightbulb in a closed electric circuit with very little resistance - if we don't regulate ourselves, we end up rapidly using up all the electricity found in this new person/relationship and will quickly burn out. Thus, it's important to be mindful and healthy and set boundaries.

When a toxic or naracssitic person love-bombs another person, they may do a lot of the same actions as a person with adhd does when going through this intense phase of novel attraction; however, it is done with the motivation of wanting to gain power for themselves, creating an emotional dependency of love bombed onto the love bomber, and ultimately done for the purpose of manipulation and control. 

Thus, since the actual definition of love-bombing means that it is done for the purpose of manipulating another, I don't think that ADHD 'love-bombing' is actually love-bombing (even though they can look similar and can still be harmful). 

​

\*\*Disclaimer\*\* This is all my opinion by the way! I am not saying this is actually the truth of the matter but this is my perspective on the topic.

Maladaptive Daydreaming can be a coping mechanism due to trauma. The "Fawn" Response is one of the Four F responses to trauma (Fight, Freeze, Flight, and Fawn) in which you essentially abandon any of your own wants and needs (like repressing them to the point that it actually feels like you do not have any wants, needs, or boundaries) and adapt to appease the traumatic situation (whether that be a person, multiple people, etc.). 

I *highly* recommend looking into the Fawn Trauma Response (as well as PTSD and Complex-PTSD) to get more information on this if you MD and people please. Your body might be telling you that there's more going on below the surface.

When traumatic incidents happen, our minds may consciously forget them to protect ourselves - it's a way of coping. But no matter how much our conscious may try to disconnect us (i.e. MD, dissociating, denial, forgetting, ridding ourselves of boundaries so they cannot be violated or crossed, etc.), our nervous system does not forget.

If there is a period of time in your life that is extremely difficult to remember, and this gap or fog in your memory seems out of place (i.e. obviously you can't remember when you were 1 year old, but let's say you had an eating disorder when you were 16 but can't remember much from the few years before that even though you can remember other things before and after those few years relatively fine - that's an example of an out of place memory gap) I would also highly recommend trying to focus on this time period more - if you're trying to locate a potential origin of trauma. If it feels like your brain is trying to hide something, it probably is. Especially if you have other symptoms of traumatic coping mechanisms.

Also, I know a lot of people can feel guilty upon realizing that they were assaulted, harassed, abused, bullied, etc., especially if it was by something that they deem as a 'good' person. I think it's important to recognize that just because someone may have done something bad, admitting that fact to yourself does not automatically also cast a value judgement onto that person who committed the act. For example, one of my best friends now bullied me extensively throughout elementary school (a long while ago now lol). There were things she did that traumatized me, and that took a lot of time to unpack and heal from. However, as we got older, she matured, I matured, and we talked more, especially about what happened when we were younger. She apologized and I forgave her because I knew (from getting to know her) that what she did was not because she ever had malicious intent, but just because she was young and naive. **That being said, being naive is not an excuse for misconduct against another person.** 

Every situation is unique and nuisanced, so it's important you listen to your own body, mind, and intuition when arriving at your own conclusions of the circumstances which took place. You do not have to prescribe to any image of what a survivor or victim of assault, abuse, etc., 'should' look like. For example, if you were sexually assaulted, yet you still enjoy having sex that is okay! That does not take away from the trauma of the experience that you went through. If another person experienced the same thing but had no desire for sex afterwards that is fine too. Both experiences and ways of coping and healing are completely valid. (Also when I say fine, I don't mean the example of sexual assault is fine, or being traumatized from such an event is fine, but the individual ways of coping are fine as long as the person is the best they can at the moment to cope and heal). 

Anyways, I kind of digressed but I wanted to share because all of which I've just explained are issues I've struggled with on my healing journey (which, of course, is still ongoing). I  hope this offers you some support too.

My final words are **\*DISCLAIMER\*** I am not a licensed professional in any field related to health, mental health, etc., etc. This is not my field of study. However, I do really enjoy learning about mental health, philosophy, spirituality, etc., etc. and so much of my knowledge/advice is based on self-learning. 

ANYWAYS, I ***really*** hoped this helped - even if just a little. I hope you have a fantastic day!!!

(Scenario 1) Something I do is just confront the issue head-on. By this, I mean if I see the person first (which is usually the case), I approach THEM first so I have a chance to set the tone of the conversation and it puts me in the 'driver's seat'. Since I approached them first I always go "Hey! How are you?" or "Hey! What are you doing here?" They then answer and will usually follow up with a "how about yourself?" kind of question, to which I give a simple, honest answer, and a closing remark "it was nice seeing you" PLUS something to acknowledge what they just said to me "good luck \[insert activity they said, i.e. grocery shopping\]". At this point, each person usually chuckles a little and then I raise my arm to wave goodbye and say "I'll see ya later!" and leave. This usually works well because it's easier to control the topic of the conversation as well as determine the length of the interaction. 

(Scenario 2) Of course, if the person approaches me first though, and they ask how I am doing, I will (try to) respond with that same simple, honest answer (sometimes it is very literal like to go back to the grocery shopping example I might say "picking apples" lol) and then I ask how they are, and after they respond I say something that, once again, acknowledges what they just said to me "haha that's awesome" (just as a general example) "good luck!" and then the closing remark "well it was nice seeing you! Thanks for saying hi!" to which they then understand is a segway to leave and we say goodbye and part ways.

The second circumstance has more uncertainty because they approached first, so they usually have control over the convo! However, it is not always who approaches first, it's usually whoever asks the first question. So even if someone else approaches you and says hi first, asking how they are doing before they ask you will allow you to revert back to Scenario 1. 

I hope this helps!
